title: Lesson 37: Asynchronous Apex: Batch, Queueable, Scheduled, and Future, and How to Choose
description: How to choose between future methods, queueable Apex, batch Apex, and scheduled Apex on evidence rather than habit, and why all four draw from one shared asynchronous budget.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Asynchronous Apex: Batch, Queueable, Scheduled, and Future, and How to Choose”, a nightly process must reconcile 40,000 Accounts against an ERP, retry failures on the next night’s run, and report a total. Which primitive and pattern fit?
options: A single @Future(callout=true) method that iterates all 40,000 accounts, because future methods run in their own transaction with a larger budget.
Batch Apex with a Database.Stateful counter and a status flag on each record so failed ones are picked up next run, kicked off by a schedulable.
One queueable job per account, enqueued in a loop, so each record’s retry is isolated in its own transaction.
A scheduled class whose execute method performs the reconciliation and the callouts directly, since scheduled Apex is asynchronous.
questions.explanation: Batch Apex is the primitive for volume and gives chunk-level fault isolation, a stateful counter carries the total across chunks, and the scheduler exists only to start it.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: Enqueueing one job per record while iterating a 50,000-record query spends the shared 24-hour async ceiling in proportion to record count and hits the 50-job-per-transaction enqueue cap, so the work gets chunked before anything is enqueued.
Queueable jobs each run in their own transaction, so one job per record is the safest design for isolated retries.
Future methods are the better default for new work because they return a job Id that can be queried for status.
Because asynchronous limits are far higher than synchronous ones, the daily asynchronous ceiling behaves as a per-feature budget rather than an org-level one.
questions.explanation: The async ceiling and the per-transaction enqueue cap are both org-level, so a job per record multiplies the shared budget by the record count; chunk first, then enqueue.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: A schedulable should perform its own heavy queries and callouts, because scheduled Apex runs asynchronously and therefore gets asynchronous limits.
Batch Apex can call a future method from its execute method when a single chunk needs callout isolation.
Database.Stateful exists to carry large record collections between chunks.
Scheduled Apex runs under tight synchronous-style limits, so its execute body should be a one-line handoff that starts a batch job or enqueues a queueable.
questions.explanation: The scheduler holds the clock and nothing else: it hands off to a batch job or a queueable, which is where the higher asynchronous budget and the real work live.
